the use of a workflow scheduler alone is insufficient in order to achieve optimal performance in a distributed system, and that the inclusion of performance modelling and batch queue wait time prediction is necessary in order to achieve good performance in such settings.

(1) the wait time for jobs submitted to batch queues is often longer than the execution time of the job itself, (2) a workflow scheduler that is aware of the batch queue wait time can improve the overall workflow execution time by 30% or more over the case where the scheduler does not know the wait time, and (3) the wait time is highly predictable

1) the performance of an individual application on a particular machine can be estimated with reasonable accuracy, 2) the amount of time a job will spend in a batch queue can be predicted with reasonable accuracy, and 3) the combination of these two predictions allows a workflow scheduler to make better decisions about where to place workflow tasks, thus reducing the total time required to execute the workflow.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a workflow scheduler that can take advantage of the performance characteristics of a given system in order to schedule workflow tasks on machines where they can be executed quickly, and to predict the amount of time tasks will spend waiting for resources to be available.
developing methods for improving the execution time of workflows on large-scale distributed systems.

the development of methods which allow workflow schedulers to accurately predict batch queue wait times and application performance, and to make use of this information when deciding where to run workflow tasks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of the workflow scheduler with performance and queue wait time prediction is beneficial for workflow scheduling, and that the performance and queue wait prediction is a necessary component of a workflow scheduler in order to achieve optimal performance in an environment that includes batch queue scheduling.
the performance of a workflow scheduler can be improved by incorporating a wait time prediction model.

the workflow scheduler we describe, when used in conjunction with the batch queue wait time prediction and performance modelling methods we introduce, is capable of producing better workflow execution times in settings where the batch queues of the underlying distributed systems impose significant delays on the execution of individual workflow tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of a workflow scheduler alone can improve performance by 1) reducing the amount of data transferred between nodes in the cluster, and 2) improving the use of the network bandwidth by scheduling tasks on nodes with similar network topology.

the performance of workflow execution on large-scale distributed systems can be significantly improved if we can accurately predict both the performance of applications on specific hardware, as well as the amount of time each task will spend waiting in queues.

the performance of the workflow scheduler can be improved significantly by using performance models to predict the performance of individual tasks on individual systems and by using queue wait time models to predict the time that individual tasks will spend waiting on batch queues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the batch queue wait time of a workflow can be accurately predicted, and that this wait time can have a dramatic effect on the performance of workflow scheduling.

, in order to make accurate predictions of workflow execution time, it is necessary to take into account the fact that most supercomputers employ batch queues, and the fact that batch queue wait times are often significant.
the scheduling of workflows on modern distributed HPC systems requires a careful consideration of the batch queue wait times of individual tasks, as well as the overall performance of the workflow.
